title: Title and occasion
short: Burns's ode, sent to George Thomson in late summer 1793 as Bruce's address to his army before Bannockburn (1314).
body: Burns wrote to Thomson that the old tune 'Hey tuttie taitie' was said by tradition to have been Robert Bruce's march at Bannockburn, and that the thought, in his solitary wanderings, roused him to an enthusiasm 'on the theme of liberty and independence', which he threw into a Scots ode imagined as the king's address to his men. The Morgan Library holds an autograph headed 'Robert Bruce's March to Bannockburn', catalogued as 30 August 1793, which explains the archive's title. John Syme gave a rival account, placing its composition on a stormy tour of Galloway in July 1793; Henley and Henderson find the two stories irreconcilable.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes
Morgan Library & Museum, autograph manuscript 'Robert Bruce's March to Bannockburn', catalogued as [30 Aug. 1793]

title: Wallace
short: Sir William Wallace (d. 1305), leader of Scottish resistance to Edward I, victor at Stirling Bridge (1297), executed in London.
body: Wallace led the rising against English occupation in 1297 and defeated an English army at Stirling Bridge, but was beaten at Falkirk in 1298 and later betrayed, taken to London and executed in 1305. The 'Scots, wha hae wi' Wallace bled' are those who fought and bled under him, now under Bruce. For Burns and his contemporaries Wallace was the type of the patriot martyr.

anchor: Scots, wham Bruce has aften led
title: Bruce
short: Robert I (Robert the Bruce, 1274-1329), crowned King of Scots in 1306, who defeated Edward II at Bannockburn.
body: Bruce seized the throne in 1306 and fought a long guerrilla war before the decisive victory at Bannockburn near Stirling on 23-24 June 1314. The English king he faced was Edward II, son of Edward I. Bruce is the speaker of the whole song.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes
'Battle of Bannockburn', Wikipedia

title: gory bed ... Or to Victorie!
short: Death in battle or victory: the stark alternative with which the speech opens.
body: The 'gory bed' is the bloody grave of the battlefield. Bruce greets his men with the choice of death or victory, which the last line ('Let us Do or Die!') repeats as a slogan. Spellings such as 'Victorie' and 'Slaverie' give a Scots flavour (and a stressed final syllable for the tune) to verse that is otherwise largely English. The bleak welcome is a rhetorical device: by naming death first, the speaker makes it a thing to be faced, not feared.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes

anchor: See the front o’ battle lour
title: lour
short: To frown or look threatening, like a darkening sky.
body: 'Lour' (or 'lower') means to scowl or to look dark and menacing, used especially of weather and faces. The 'front o' battle' is the advancing English line, which darkens like a storm. The urgent repetitions ('Now's the day, and now's the hour'; 'See ... See') give the stanza the pace of an address in the moment of crisis. The word links the moral climate of the battle with weather, a common figure in heroic poetry.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'lour'

title: proud Edward
short: Edward II of England (r. 1307-27), whose large army was defeated at Bannockburn.
body: Edward II led a large English army to relieve Stirling Castle in 1314. 'Power' here means armed force, host. The line ends in the cry 'Chains and Slaverie!', what defeat would bring.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes

title: 'Struggles not quite so ancient'
short: Burns told Thomson that the ode was inspired also by 'other struggles of the same nature, not quite so ancient': the 1790s.
body: Henley and Henderson quote Burns's admission that the song was prompted by the glowing ideas of 'some other struggles of the same nature not quite so ancient', and conclude that it is partly an effect of the French Revolution. In 1793 Britain was at war with France and the government was prosecuting Scottish radicals: the trial of the reformer Thomas Muir began on 30 August 1793. Read in that light, the rhetoric of chains, tyrants and usurpers addresses the present as much as 1314, which is why Burns, a government exciseman, published it anonymously.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes
'Scots Wha Hae' annotation, The Traditional Tune Archive (on Burns's letter and the Muir trial)

anchor: Wha will be a traitor knave?
title: The rhetorical questions
short: Three questions in a row shame any coward; the answer is in the command 'Let him turn and flee!'
body: The third stanza is built on anaphora (repeated 'Wha ...'), a device of classical oratory. Each question names a disgrace: treachery, a 'coward's grave', and slavery. The fourth stanza answers with the positive counterpart ('Wha, for Scotland's King and Law ...'), so the song moves in paired stanzas from shame to resolve. Rhetorically, the questions exclude the unworthy before the battle, as heroic speakers in epic and history often do; the man who would rather be a slave is told to turn and run.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes

title: Free-man stand, or Free-man fa'
short: Whether he lives or dies, he will do so as a free man: the song's ideal of liberty.
body: The chiasmic balance of 'stand ... fa'' (fall) makes freedom independent of the outcome: the free man is free whether he survives or not. 'Scotland's King and Law' joins loyalty to lawful government with national independence, a careful formulation in the 1790s, when 'Liberty' was a dangerous word. The capitalised 'Free-man' recurs as a title of dignity, opposed to the 'Slave' of the previous stanza. The line's compression, with the subject repeated and the verbs in balance, gives it the force of a motto.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes

anchor: By your Sons in servile chains!
title: By Oppression's woes ... servile chains
short: An oath by present and future suffering: if the battle is lost, their sons will be enslaved.
body: The fifth stanza takes the form of an oath ('By ... By ...'), common in heroic speeches. 'Servile' (from Latin servus, slave) chains belong to slaves. 'We will drain our dearest veins' is a vow to shed their own blood so that their sons may be free. The stanza widens the stakes from the soldiers to their descendants, so that the battle becomes a fight for future generations, a standard theme of patriotic oratory. 'They shall be free!' is a prophecy as well as a vow.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'servile'

title: Usurpers ... Tyrants
short: The English invaders, who claim a crown not theirs; the words were charged in 1790s political language.
body: A usurper seizes power to which he has no right. Burns, writing to Lord Buchan, called the English king 'a cruel, but able usurper' leading the finest army in Europe. 'Tyrants fall in every foe' means that each enemy killed is a tyrant overthrown. These words, with 'Liberty', were the vocabulary of the revolutionary decade. The exclamations of the final stanza are almost entirely abstract nouns and imperatives, the language of the political ode rather than of the ballad.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes

title: Liberty's in every blow!
short: Each stroke struck is a blow for freedom; Burns wrote to Lord Buchan that liberty can never be too dearly bought.
body: Henley and Henderson quote Burns's letter to the Earl of Buchan sending him a copy, in which he says that nothing in history moves him more than Bannockburn, and that Liberty is a prize that 'never canst thou be too dearly bought'. The line distils that sentiment into four words of action. The shift from 'Freedom' to 'Liberty' in the last stanza gives the ode the vocabulary of the age of revolutions, in which 'Liberty' was the watchword of France and of British reformers.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes

title: Do or Die
short: The final rallying cry: succeed or perish. The capitals stress a phrase that became a proverbial motto.
body: 'Do or die' was already an English phrase for a desperate resolve, and Burns's use of it as the climax of the song made it famous as a Scottish rallying cry. The close returns to the opening alternative of 'gory bed' or 'Victorie'. The song became an unofficial national anthem of Scotland. The capital letters, as printed in the archive's text, emphasise the slogan; in performance the line is often sung with special force.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'do'

title: Stanza and tune
short: Trochaic lines with three rhymes and a short fourth line, written to the air 'Hey tuttie taitie'; Thomson made Burns lengthen it for 'Lewie Gordon'.
body: Each stanza has three rhyming four-stress lines and a short refrain-like fourth line. Thomson disliked 'Hey tuttie taitie' and persuaded Burns to add words to each fourth line so that it would fit 'Lewie Gordon'. After Burns's death opinion favoured the original, and Thomson printed the ode as first written, to its own air, in 1802; Henley and Henderson follow that text.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes
National Trust for Scotland collections, 'Tune, Lewis Gordon' (Burns's revision for Thomson)

title: Anonymous first printing
short: First printed in the Morning Chronicle (London) in May 1794, as if found by accident and without the author's knowledge.
body: Burns allowed James Perry of the Morning Chronicle, a Whig paper sympathetic to reform, to print the ode provided it appeared as something 'met with by accident and unknown to me'. The paper prefaced it with praise for a faithful imitation of the old Scottish bards and hinted that only one living poet could have written it. As a government excise officer suspected of radical sympathies, Burns had reason to be careful.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes

anchor: Wha, for Scotland’s King and Law
title: Scots or English?
short: The ode is largely eighteenth-century English with Scots spellings.
body: Words like 'wha', 'wham', 'aften', 'sae' and 'fa'' are Scots spellings, but the grammar, diction and rhetoric (abstract nouns such as Oppression, Liberty, Usurpers) are those of the English ode. This sits oddly with the Morning Chronicle's claim that it imitated the old bards. The blend suits a song meant for national and political use beyond Scotland.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes
